title: Antioxidants and Free Radical Scavengers
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Aerobic life runs on the stepwise reduction of oxygen, and every partially reduced intermediate along the way is chemically aggressive. This chapter explains how superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radical are generated, how they injure lipids, proteins, and DNA, and how a layered defense of enzymes, small-molecule scavengers, and melanin contains them. It then applies the same chemistry in two directions: ultraviolet injury and photoaging in skin, and the deliberate use of reactive oxygen species by neutrophils to kill microbes. Board questions here ask you to follow electrons from a source to a lesion, or from a missing enzyme to a predictable disease.
prerequisites: Mitochondrial electron transport, including the roles of complexes I and III and coenzyme Q
The pentose phosphate pathway and the regulation of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Membrane structure and the chemistry of polyunsaturated fatty acids
DNA repair pathways, especially base excision repair and nucleotide excision repair
Epidermal layers, melanocyte biology, and dermal collagen and elastic fiber architecture (IN-1, IN-5)

connections.how: Mature erythrocytes have no mitochondria, so the pentose phosphate pathway is their only source of NADPH, which makes G6PD deficiency a hemolytic disease driven purely by oxidant stress.
The same NADPH oxidase chemistry that damages host tissue is the neutrophil's primary microbicidal weapon, so losing it produces a specific and predictable infection pattern.
Oxidative and photochemical DNA lesions that escape repair become the signature mutations of actinic keratosis, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma.
Selenium, riboflavin, zinc, copper, and manganese are cofactors for antioxidant enzymes, and vitamins C and E work in the same radical-quenching network as glutathione and ubiquinol.
The matrix metalloproteinases that remodel a healing wound are the ones ultraviolet signaling turns on chronically in photoaged dermis.

terms.def: Any species with an unpaired electron in an outer orbital, which makes it reactive and able to propagate damage by taking an electron or hydrogen atom from a neighbor.
Oxygen-derived oxidants, including the radicals superoxide and hydroxyl radical and the non-radicals hydrogen peroxide and singlet oxygen.
A state in which oxidant production exceeds antioxidant capacity, shifting the cell's redox balance toward oxidation and allowing damage to accumulate.
Reduction of hydrogen peroxide by ferrous iron (Fe2+) to yield hydroxyl radical, hydroxide ion, and ferric iron (Fe3+).
A reaction in which two identical molecules are converted to two different products, one more oxidized and one more reduced, as when two superoxide anions yield hydrogen peroxide and oxygen.
A self-propagating chain reaction in which a radical abstracts hydrogen from a polyunsaturated fatty acid, and the resulting peroxyl radical attacks the next fatty acid.
A covalent four-carbon ring linking two adjacent pyrimidines on the same DNA strand, formed when UVB is absorbed directly by the bases.
An excited, non-radical form of molecular oxygen produced when a photoexcited pigment transfers energy to oxygen; it attacks double bonds directly.
A molecule that absorbs light and passes the energy or an electron to another molecule, generating reactive species without being consumed itself.
The abrupt rise in oxygen consumption by an activated phagocyte as NADPH oxidase reduces oxygen to superoxide inside the phagosome.
Accumulation of amorphous, blue-gray (basophilic) degenerated collagen and elastic material in the upper dermis of chronically sun-exposed skin.

sections.title: Formation of reactive oxygen species and the lesions they leave

blocks.text: Molecular oxygen is a poor one-electron acceptor but an excellent four-electron acceptor, which is what cytochrome c oxidase provides when it reduces O2 to water. Trouble begins whenever oxygen is reduced one electron at a time, because each partial reduction leaves a species more reactive than the one before it: superoxide, then hydrogen peroxide, then hydroxyl radical, and only then water.

Superoxide is the usual entry point. A small fraction of the electrons moving through mitochondrial complexes I and III escapes onto oxygen instead of continuing down the chain, and this leak rises when the chain is reduced and the proton-motive force is high. Phagocytes make superoxide deliberately through NADPH oxidase (C05), and related NOX isoforms in keratinocytes and fibroblasts generate it as a signaling molecule. Superoxide is only moderately reactive, but it inactivates iron-sulfur cluster enzymes, releases free iron, and combines with nitric oxide to form peroxynitrite.

Hydrogen peroxide is not a radical and is a weak oxidant, yet it is the most dangerous intermediate in practice because it is uncharged, crosses membranes, and travels well away from where it formed. Its hazard is what ferrous iron does to it: the Fenton reaction splits hydrogen peroxide into hydroxyl radical, hydroxide, and ferric iron, and superoxide reduces that ferric iron back to the ferrous state so the cycle continues. Hydroxyl radical then reacts within a few molecular diameters, damaging whatever lies next to where it formed, which is why iron overload, hemolysis, and free heme amplify oxidative injury, and why ionizing radiation is so damaging, since it splits water directly into hydroxyl radical and hydrogen atoms. In skin, UVA adds another route by exciting endogenous photosensitizers such as riboflavin and porphyrins, which pass energy to oxygen to form singlet oxygen or an electron to form superoxide.

Superoxide dismutation: hydrogen peroxide, uncharged and membrane permeable
Hydrogen peroxide meets Fe2+: Fenton reaction yields hydroxyl radical
Hydroxyl radical attacks the nearest lipid, protein, or base
Full four-electron reduction instead yields water, with no intermediate released

blocks.text: Three targets, three signature lesions

Membrane lipids are vulnerable because the carbon between two double bonds in a polyunsaturated fatty acid holds its hydrogen weakly, so one abstraction starts the propagating chain shown below, the membrane loses its permeability barrier, and the aldehyde breakdown products carry the injury beyond the membrane.

Protein oxidation hits the side chains that carry function, so activity is lost and the altered protein is degraded by the proteasome. In DNA, 8-oxoguanine is the lesion to know: it can rotate and pair with adenine, so replication over an unrepaired lesion installs a G:C to T:A transversion unless glycosylase-initiated base excision repair removes it first. Mitochondrial DNA is hit hardest, since it sits beside the source, lacks histone protection, and has a narrower repair repertoire.

blocks.title: Three targets and their signature lesions
rows: Hydrogen abstraction, then a propagating peroxyl radical chain

Loss of function, fragmentation, lipofuscin accumulation
8-oxoguanine, thymine glycol, abasic sites, strand breaks
G:C to T:A transversion, replication arrest, instability
blocks.caption: Lipid damage spreads, protein damage is lost function, and DNA damage is heritable, which is why one oxidant produces three kinds of disease.

blocks.title: Lipid peroxidation as a chain reaction
steps: Radical abstracts hydrogen from the bis-allylic carbon of a polyunsaturated fatty acid
Lipid radical adds O2 to form a lipid peroxyl radical
Peroxyl radical abstracts hydrogen from the adjacent fatty acid: propagation
Chain continues until vitamin E, ubiquinol, or glutathione peroxidase 4 intervenes
Malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal form and cross-link proteins and DNA
blocks.caption: Propagation is why a single initiating radical can oxidize hundreds of fatty acids, and why chain-breaking antioxidants matter more than their numbers suggest.

sections.title: Antioxidant enzymes and why glutathione depends on G6PD

blocks.text: Enzymatic defense is a relay, and its logic is that hydrogen peroxide must be destroyed before it meets ferrous iron. Superoxide dismutase accelerates the dismutation of two superoxide anions into hydrogen peroxide and oxygen, which looks counterproductive until you notice that it converts a species no downstream enzyme can handle into one that two enzymes can. Its three isoforms sit in three compartments, which matters because superoxide cannot cross a membrane to reach an enzyme elsewhere.

Hydrogen peroxide is then removed two ways. Catalase, a heme-containing tetramer abundant in peroxisomes and in erythrocyte cytosol, converts two molecules of hydrogen peroxide into two of water and one of oxygen; its affinity for substrate is low, so it dominates when peroxide concentrations are high. Glutathione peroxidase carries selenium as selenocysteine in its active site, spends two molecules of reduced glutathione to reduce hydrogen peroxide to water, and works efficiently at the low concentrations of routine metabolism. Its isoform glutathione peroxidase 4 is the only enzyme that reduces peroxidized fatty acids while they remain esterified in the membrane, so it is the dedicated brake on lipid peroxidation.

blocks.title: The antioxidant enzymes
rows: 2 superoxide plus 2 H+ to hydrogen peroxide plus O2
Same dismutation at the main site of generation
2 hydrogen peroxide to 2 water plus O2
Hydrogen peroxide plus 2 GSH to 2 water plus GSSG
Reduces esterified lipid hydroperoxides to alcohols
GSSG plus NADPH plus H+ to 2 GSH plus NADP+
blocks.caption: Note the nutritional dependencies: copper, zinc, manganese, iron as heme, selenium, and riboflavin as FAD.

blocks.text: Glutathione peroxidase consumes its reductant, so the system is only as good as its ability to regenerate reduced glutathione. Glutathione reductase does that using NADPH, which in most cells comes largely from the oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, where glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step. G6PD is regulated exactly as this logic predicts: NADP+ activates it and NADPH inhibits it, so spending NADPH on glutathione recycling immediately increases flux.

blocks.title: The glutathione antioxidant cycle and its NADPH supply
steps: G6PD oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate, generating NADPH
Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to convert GSSG to 2 GSH
Selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase uses 2 GSH to reduce hydrogen peroxide to water
GSH is oxidized back to GSSG as its thiols form a disulfide
Rising NADP+ relieves inhibition of G6PD and the cycle accelerates
blocks.caption: Glutathione is recycled rather than consumed, so a small pool handles a large oxidant load as long as NADPH keeps arriving.

blocks.text: The mature erythrocyte shows what happens when this one supply line fails. With no mitochondria and no nucleus, it depends entirely on the pentose phosphate pathway and cannot synthesize new enzyme. In G6PD deficiency, an X-linked recessive disorder, baseline function is adequate but an oxidant challenge from infection, certain sulfonamides and antimalarials, or fava beans outstrips NADPH supply. Glutathione falls, hemoglobin oxidizes and denatures into inclusions seen as Heinz bodies on supravital staining, and splenic macrophages bite pieces from those cells, giving the bite cells of an acute episodic hemolysis. The network is also inducible: oxidation of reactive cysteines on Keap1 releases the transcription factor Nrf2, which raises transcription of glutamate-cysteine ligase, heme oxygenase 1, and glutathione S-transferases, so a mild exposure strengthens the response to the next one.

blocks.title: Following one molecule of hydrogen peroxide
blocks.text: A keratinocyte generates one hydrogen peroxide molecule. Glutathione peroxidase reduces it to water, oxidizing two glutathione molecules into one GSSG, and glutathione reductase then spends one NADPH to restore both. That NADPH came from one turn of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, so one peroxide costs one NADPH and peroxide-handling capacity is set by glucose-6-phosphate flux. Remove selenium and the peroxidase cannot run; remove G6PD activity and the cycle stalls one step later. Either way the peroxide survives to meet ferrous iron, which is why a nutritional deficiency and an enzyme deficiency produce the same injury.

blocks.predict: Superoxide dismutase produces hydrogen peroxide. Why does overexpressing it alone, without extra catalase or glutathione peroxidase, fail to protect a cell?
blocks.explain: Dismutation only moves the problem one step down the chain. More superoxide dismutase means more hydrogen peroxide, and hydrogen peroxide is membrane permeable and feeds the Fenton reaction. Protection requires matched downstream capacity to destroy the peroxide before it meets ferrous iron.

sections.title: Non-vitamin antioxidants of skin: glutathione, ubiquinol, carotenoids, and melanin

blocks.text: Enzymes handle defined substrates, so the cell also keeps a pool of small molecules that can absorb a radical wherever it appears, and the solubility of each one decides where it works.

Glutathione is the tripeptide gamma-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine, and its two unusual features both serve its function. The gamma-glutamyl linkage is not a normal peptide bond, so ordinary peptidases cannot degrade it, and the cysteine thiol is the reactive group that donates a hydrogen atom to a radical or an electron pair to glutathione peroxidase. Cytosolic glutathione is held at roughly a hundred to one in favor of the reduced form, so the ratio itself reads out redox state. Synthesis takes two ATP-dependent steps, of which glutamate-cysteine ligase is rate limiting, and cysteine availability usually sets the ceiling. Glutathione also conjugates electrophiles through glutathione S-transferases, which is how skin disposes of reactive products of lipid peroxidation.

Ubiquinol is the reduced form of coenzyme Q10, a benzoquinone ring with a ten-isoprene tail that anchors it in the hydrophobic core of membranes. There it donates hydrogen to lipid peroxyl radicals, breaking the propagation chain described in C01, and it regenerates alpha-tocopherol from the tocopheroxyl radical left when vitamin E does the same job. Carotenoids protect by different chemistry: their long conjugated polyene backbone accepts the excitation energy of singlet oxygen, dropping the oxygen to its ground state, and then releases that energy as heat and survives intact. Lycopene is acyclic and lacks the beta-ionone ring, so unlike beta-carotene it has no provitamin A activity. Carotenoids deposit in the stratum corneum and subcutaneous fat, and heavy intake yields a yellow-orange discoloration that spares the sclera, which distinguishes it from jaundice.

blocks.text: Melanin is the skin's structural sunscreen. Melanocytes in the basal layer synthesize it inside melanosomes from tyrosine by way of dopaquinone, the first steps being catalyzed by the copper-dependent enzyme tyrosinase, then transfer the granules to keratinocytes, where they form caps over the nuclei. The pathway branches at dopaquinone according to cysteine availability. With little cysteine, dopaquinone cyclizes toward the indole intermediates that polymerize into eumelanin, a brown-black broadband absorber that converts most of the ultraviolet energy it takes up into heat and scavenges radicals through its stable semiquinone groups. With abundant cysteine, dopaquinone instead forms cysteinyldopa and then pheomelanin, a red-yellow sulfur-containing polymer that absorbs ultraviolet poorly, is photolabile, and under UVA acts as a photosensitizer generating superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, so it adds to the oxidant burden rather than only protecting less. Loss-of-function variants in the melanocortin 1 receptor, which give red hair and fair skin, shift synthesis toward pheomelanin and also blunt receptor-dependent signaling that supports DNA repair, which is why that phenotype carries a higher melanoma risk.

blocks.predict: Two people receive the same ultraviolet dose. One has densely pigmented eumelanic skin, the other red hair and pheomelanic skin. Why is the difference in oxidative DNA damage larger than the difference in pigment quantity alone would suggest?
blocks.explain: Eumelanin absorbs across the ultraviolet range and dissipates that energy as heat while quenching radicals, so it subtracts from the oxidant load. Pheomelanin absorbs poorly and, once excited, generates superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, so it adds to the load. The two pigments move the balance in opposite directions, and reduced melanocortin 1 receptor signaling further weakens repair.
blocks.check: The dopaquinone branch point in this section and the ultraviolet damage mechanisms in C04.

sections.title: UVB versus UVA injury and the mechanism of photoaging

blocks.text: Ultraviolet wavelength determines two things at once: how deep the photons travel and what absorbs them. Shorter wavelengths are absorbed more superficially but match the absorption spectrum of DNA, while longer wavelengths penetrate further and must work through intermediary pigments. UVC, below about 280 nm, is absorbed by stratospheric ozone and does not reach the skin from sunlight.

UVB is directly genotoxic. DNA bases absorb these photons themselves, and the excited state lets two adjacent pyrimidines on one strand join through their carbon 5 and carbon 6 positions as a cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer, or less often a pyrimidine-pyrimidone (6-4) photoproduct. Either lesion distorts the helix and blocks replication and transcription, and both are removed by nucleotide excision repair; inherited failure of that pathway produces xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme photosensitivity and early skin cancer. Unrepaired dimers are copied with error, giving the signature C to T transitions at dipyrimidine sites and CC to TT tandem mutations found in TP53 in actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma and in PTCH1 in basal cell carcinoma. Clinically UVB causes sunburn: keratinocytes damaged beyond repair undergo p53-dependent apoptosis and appear as sunburn cells with shrunken nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, while prostaglandins, cytokines, and nitric oxide produce the erythema and edema that peak hours later. UVB also drives delayed tanning, since p53 raises keratinocyte proopiomelanocortin and the alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone released acts on melanocortin 1 receptors.

UVA is mostly indirectly genotoxic. It is absorbed by endogenous photosensitizers rather than by DNA, generating singlet oxygen and superoxide that leave oxidative lesions such as 8-oxoguanine and strand breaks, repaired by base excision repair instead. Because it reaches the dermis, UVA is the main source of injury to fibroblasts, collagen, and elastic fibers, and it produces immediate pigment darkening by oxidizing and redistributing existing melanin rather than making new pigment.

blocks.title: UVB and UVA compared
rows: Photosensitizers that transfer energy to oxygen
Actinic keratosis, squamous and basal cell carcinoma
blocks.caption: The mnemonic UVA for aging and UVB for burning is accurate as long as you remember both contribute to cancer.

blocks.text: Photoaging is a connective tissue disease caused by signaling, not by photons breaking collagen directly. As the figure below traces, reactive oxygen species generated in the dermis activate mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades and with them the transcription factor AP-1, which does two additive things: it induces matrix metalloproteinases, chiefly MMP-1 (interstitial collagenase), and it interferes with transforming growth factor beta signaling so that procollagen synthesis falls. Degradation rises while replacement falls, and each exposure leaves a small permanent deficit. Histologically, chronically exposed dermis shows solar elastosis: amorphous blue-gray degenerated collagen and tangled thickened elastic material in the upper dermis, with epidermal atrophy and flattening of the dermal-epidermal junction. Clinically this is coarse deep wrinkling, yellow leathery thickening, laxity, telangiectasia, and solar lentigines, which differs from intrinsic aging, where the dermis thins with fine wrinkles and no elastotic deposit.

AP-1 induces MMP-1, MMP-3, and MMP-9
AP-1 also blocks TGF-beta signaling, lowering procollagen synthesis

Coarse wrinkling, laxity, and leathery yellow skin

sections.title: The respiratory burst, myeloperoxidase, and chronic granulomatous disease

blocks.text: Phagocytes turn the chemistry of oxidative injury into a weapon. When a neutrophil engulfs a microbe, the cytosolic components of NADPH oxidase assemble onto the membrane flavocytochrome already in the phagosome wall, which is the gp91phox and p22phox pair, and the completed enzyme transfers electrons from cytosolic NADPH through FAD and two heme groups to oxygen in the phagosome lumen, generating superoxide. Oxygen consumption rises sharply, which is why the event is called the respiratory burst, and the NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway, the same source that serves glutathione. Because the oxidase moves electrons across a membrane without moving a counter-ion, the phagosome would quickly become too electronegative to continue; a voltage-gated proton channel compensates.

The products are then escalated. Superoxide dismutates to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase, released from azurophilic granules and intensely green because of its heme, uses that peroxide with chloride to generate hypochlorous acid, the active ingredient of household bleach. Hypochlorous acid chlorinates and oxidizes microbial proteins and lipids indiscriminately and is the most potent microbicidal product the neutrophil makes; the same pigment gives pus its green color. The burst also activates granule proteases, so oxidative and non-oxidative killing act together.

blocks.title: The neutrophil respiratory burst
steps: Phagosome forms around the microbe and the oxidase subunits assemble
NADPH oxidase moves electrons from NADPH onto O2: superoxide in the lumen
Proton channel balances the charge so transfer continues
Superoxide dismutates to hydrogen peroxide, spontaneously and enzymatically
Myeloperoxidase combines hydrogen peroxide with chloride: hypochlorous acid
Oxidation and chlorination kill the microbe, aided by activated granule proteases
blocks.caption: Each step is the same chemistry described in C01, confined to a compartment where the damage is intended.

blocks.text: Chronic granulomatous disease is loss of this oxidase. About two thirds of cases are X-linked, from mutations in CYBB encoding the gp91phox membrane subunit, and the remainder are autosomal recessive, most commonly in p47phox. Phagocytosis and degranulation are intact, so microbes are ingested but survive inside the cell. Patients present in early childhood with recurrent suppurative infection of the skin, lymph nodes, lungs, liver, and bone, with abscess formation and suppurative adenitis. Granulomas form because ingested organisms and debris persist, so macrophages and T cells wall them off, and in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts these masses can obstruct. The organisms that cause trouble are classically catalase-positive, as the comparison below lists. The usual teaching explanation is that catalase-negative organisms generate hydrogen peroxide of their own that the neutrophil's myeloperoxidase can borrow, whereas catalase-positive organisms destroy their own peroxide and leave the phagocyte with nothing. Diagnosis rests on showing an absent burst: dihydrorhodamine 123 flow cytometry is the quantitative test, and the older nitroblue tetrazolium slide test stays colorless instead of turning blue.

Myeloperoxidase deficiency shows how specific these lesions are. It is the commonest inherited neutrophil enzyme defect and is usually asymptomatic, because superoxide and hydrogen peroxide are still produced and other killing mechanisms compensate; disseminated candidal infection occurs mainly in patients who are also diabetic. The nitroblue tetrazolium test is normal, since the burst itself is intact and only the conversion to hypochlorous acid is lost. The dihydrorhodamine assay is the exception worth knowing, because oxidation of dihydrorhodamine 123 to fluorescent rhodamine is itself peroxidase dependent, so severe myeloperoxidase deficiency can lower the signal and mimic chronic granulomatous disease on a screening test even though the oxidase works.

Catalase-positive: S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Aspergillus
Typical, may obstruct GI or GU tract

Nitroblue tetrazolium normal; dihydrorhodamine may be low because its oxidation needs peroxidase
blocks.caption: The burst is intact in myeloperoxidase deficiency, so the nitroblue tetrazolium test separates the two disorders while a low dihydrorhodamine result alone does not.

blocks.predict: A child with chronic granulomatous disease clears a streptococcal pharyngitis without difficulty but develops a liver abscess from Staphylococcus aureus. What accounts for the difference?
blocks.explain: Streptococci are catalase-negative and generate hydrogen peroxide that the neutrophil's myeloperoxidase can still convert to hypochlorous acid, so killing proceeds despite the missing oxidase. Staphylococcus aureus is catalase-positive and degrades that peroxide, leaving the phagocyte with no substrate for myeloperoxidase, so the organism survives intracellularly and is carried into tissue.

integration.text: One chemistry explains the whole chapter, and the discipline changes only with the compartment it happens in. Biochemistry supplies the electrons, since the pentose phosphate pathway feeds NADPH to glutathione reductase in a keratinocyte and to NADPH oxidase in a neutrophil, and nutrition supplies the cofactors, since selenium, copper, zinc, manganese, iron, and riboflavin are each built into an antioxidant enzyme. Anatomy and histology decide what is exposed: ultraviolet wavelength sets the depth, so the epidermis takes the direct photochemical hit while the dermis takes the oxidative one, which is why the signature lesions of photodamage are keratinocyte mutations above and degraded collagen below. Immunology shows the same reactions used on purpose, and pathology shows the cost when containment fails.

The reasoning also has limits worth stating. Reactive oxygen species are not purely toxic; hydrogen peroxide at low concentration is a genuine second messenger, the respiratory burst is indispensable, and Nrf2 signaling means a mild oxidant exposure strengthens later defense, which is part of why large doses of single antioxidants have not performed as the simple model predicts. Carotenoids themselves can act as prooxidants at high concentration and high oxygen tension. The catalase explanation for the organism pattern in chronic granulomatous disease is the standard board answer but is incompletely supported experimentally, so hold it as the expected reasoning rather than settled mechanism, and remember that bacterial virulence and intracellular niche also shape which organisms cause disease.

summary: One-electron reduction of oxygen gives superoxide, then hydrogen peroxide, then hydroxyl radical; full four-electron reduction gives water and releases nothing.
Hydrogen peroxide is the pivotal intermediate because it is uncharged and diffuses, and ferrous iron converts it to hydroxyl radical in the Fenton reaction.
Lipid peroxidation is a propagating chain on polyunsaturated fatty acids; 8-oxoguanine mispairs with adenine and yields a G:C to T:A transversion.
Superoxide dismutase is copper and zinc in the cytosol and manganese in mitochondria; catalase and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase then destroy the hydrogen peroxide.
Each peroxide reduced by glutathione peroxidase costs one NADPH, which in erythrocytes can only come from G6PD, so oxidant stress in G6PD deficiency gives Heinz bodies and bite cells.
Glutathione and ubiquinol are recycled electron donors in water and lipid compartments; carotenoids quench singlet oxygen physically, and lycopene has no provitamin A activity.
Eumelanin absorbs broadly and quenches radicals, while pheomelanin absorbs poorly and generates superoxide under UVA, so it adds to the oxidant load.
UVB is absorbed by DNA directly and forms cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers repaired by nucleotide excision repair; UVA works through photosensitizers and reaches the dermis.
Photoaging is transcriptional: reactive oxygen species activate AP-1, which raises MMP-1 and suppresses procollagen synthesis, leaving solar elastosis in the upper dermis.

Chronic granulomatous disease is loss of NADPH oxidase with abscesses and granulomas from catalase-positive organisms and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine test, while myeloperoxidase deficiency leaves the burst and those tests normal.

verify: The fraction of mitochondrial oxygen consumption that leaks to superoxide is given as 1 to 2 percent in older texts and well under 1 percent in more recent measurements; this chapter says only a small fraction. Confirm whether NABNE expects a number.
UVB and UVA boundary wavelengths are given here as about 280 to 315 nm and 315 to 400 nm; many dermatology sources use 290 to 320 nm and 320 to 400 nm. Confirm the convention NABNE uses.
The share of ground-level ultraviolet that is UVA is commonly quoted as about 95 percent, with UVB about 5 percent; sources vary with latitude and season, so this chapter states it qualitatively.
Proportion of chronic granulomatous disease that is X-linked is quoted from about 65 to 70 percent; p47phox is the commonest autosomal recessive form. Confirm the figures expected.

The catalase hypothesis for the infection pattern in chronic granulomatous disease remains the standard examination answer but has been questioned experimentally. It is presented here as the expected reasoning.

Board sources usually state simply that the dihydrorhodamine and nitroblue tetrazolium tests are normal in myeloperoxidase deficiency. The peroxidase dependence of dihydrorhodamine oxidation, which can give a low result despite an intact burst, comes from the clinical laboratory literature; confirm which version NABNE expects.
Whether NABNE Part I expects the subunit names gp91phox, p22phox, p47phox, p67phox, and p40phox with their gene symbols, or only the concept of an NADPH oxidase defect.

Whether NABNE expects the proton channel that balances charge during the respiratory burst, and whether it expects glutathione peroxidase isoform numbering such as the role of glutathione peroxidase 4 in membrane lipid hydroperoxides.
The cytosolic ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione is quoted from roughly 50:1 to over 100:1 depending on tissue and method; this chapter says roughly a hundred to one.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: ros-cascade (oxygen reduced stepwise with each removing enzyme labeled at its compartment), melanin-branch (tyrosine to dopaquinone branching to eumelanin or cysteinyldopa and pheomelanin), and uv-depth (UVB and UVA penetration depth against epidermal and dermal layers).
